name: Trimbakeshwar Temple, Trimbak
deity: Shiva as Tryambakeshwar, the three-eyed lord — one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, its three small lingas honoured as Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva
period: An ancient tirtha at the source of the Godavari; the present temple built under the Peshwas in the 18th century
summary: At the foot of Brahmagiri, where the Godavari begins its long journey east, Trimbakeshwar honours Shiva as the three-eyed lord — one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, its sanctum holding Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva together.

sections.history: Trimbak lies about 28 km from Nashik, beneath the long scarp of Brahmagiri, the hill where the Godavari rises. The Dvadasha Jyotirlinga Stotram names Tryambaka "on the bank of the Gautami", the Godavari's sacred name, among the twelve Jyotirlingas, and the town has drawn pilgrims for the rites of the river since ancient times. The temple standing today was built in the eighteenth century under the Peshwa Balaji Bajirao, known as Nanasaheb, in dark basalt within a high walled court. Trimbak is also one of the four places of the Kumbh Mela: every twelve years, in the Simhastha, the ascetic orders bathe at its Kushavarta tank, regarded as the ritual source of the Godavari.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Nagara shrine of black stone, its spire rising in clustered tiers above a mandapa and a carved gateway, the whole set in a paved courtyard enclosed by a high wall. Its outer surfaces are worked with figures, mouldings and ornament in the Maratha manner. In the sanctum the Jyotirlinga is unusual: within a hollow in the pedestal rest three small lingas, honoured as Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. On special occasions they are covered with a jewelled crown that tradition holds to be of great age.
sections.legends: The sacred story of Trimbak belongs to the sage Gautama, who lived on Brahmagiri with his wife Ahalya. When a cow died in his field, the sage sought to atone and worshipped Shiva with deep austerity, asking that the Ganga be brought to the hill to purify the land. Pleased, Shiva released the river here, and she flowed out as the Godavari, also called the Gautami after the sage. At Gautama's prayer the lord remained as Tryambaka, the three-eyed one, beside the river's source.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri brings the greatest crowds, and the Mondays of Shravan are kept with special worship. Kartik Purnima, celebrated as Tripuri Purnima, fills the town with lamps. Every twelve years the Simhastha Kumbh, held jointly with Nashik, draws vast gatherings to the Kushavarta tank. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Many pilgrims bathe or sprinkle water at Kushavarta before darshan, and the hardier climb Brahmagiri to the spring of the Godavari. Trimbak is also known for ancestral and atonement rites, performed by its hereditary priests. A short walk away is the samadhi of Sant Nivruttinath, elder brother of Sant Dnyaneshwar. Entry to the temple is restricted to Hindus; visitors of other faiths may view it from outside.

visit.timings: Open daily from early morning to night, with aartis and abhisheka through the day; queues are long at Maha Shivaratri, on Shravan Mondays and at weekends. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance, especially for rituals in the sanctum.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the temple; follow the posted rules and staff guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Trimbak is about 28 km from Nashik by road, at the foot of the Brahmagiri hills. Nashik Road is the nearest major railway station and Nashik (Ozar) the nearest airport; Mumbai is about 180 km away. Admission to the temple is for Hindus only, as posted at the entrance.
